prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Today outside your prison I stand and rattle my walking stick: Prisoners, listen; you have relatives outside. And there are thousands of ways to escape. Years ago I bent my skill to keep my cell locked, had chains smuggled to me in pies, and shouted my plans to jailers; but always new plans occured to me, or the new heavy locks bent hinges off, or some stupid jailer would forget and leave the keys. Inside, I dreamed of constellations— those feeding creatures outlined by stars, their skeletons a darkness between jewels, heroes that exist only where they are not. Thus freedom always came nibbling my thought, just as—often, in light, on the open hills— you can pass an antelope and not know and look back, and then—even before you see— there is something wrong about the grass. And then you see. That’s the way everything in the world is waiting. Now—these few more words, and then I’m gone: Tell everyone just to remember their names, and remind others, later, when we find each other. Tell the little ones to cry and then go to sleep, curled up where they can. And if any of us get lost, if any of us cannot come all the way— remember: there will come a time when all we have said and all we have hoped will be all right. There will be that form in the grass.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Today, Prisoners, And

outputs.L1:
Today, outside your prison, I stand and rattle my walking stick: Prisoners, listen—you have relatives beyond these walls, and there are thousands of ways to escape.

Years ago, I bent all my skill toward keeping my cell locked. I had chains smuggled in to me in pies and shouted my plans to the jailers. Yet new plans always occurred to me; or the new, heavy locks bent the hinges loose; or some foolish jailer, forgetting himself, would leave the keys.

Inside, I dreamed of constellations—those feeding creatures outlined by stars, their skeletons a darkness between jewels; heroes that exist only where they are not. Thus freedom was always nibbling at my thoughts, just as—often, in the light, on the open hills—you can pass an antelope without knowing it, then look back, and even before you see it, sense that something is wrong about the grass. And then you see.

That is the way everything in the world is waiting.

Now, these few more words, and then I am gone: Tell everyone simply to remember their names, and to remind others later, when we find one another. Tell the little ones to cry, and then go to sleep, curled up wherever they can.

And if any of us become lost, if any of us cannot come all the way, remember: there will come a time when all we have said and all we have hoped will be made right. There will be that form in the grass.
outputs.L2:
I am here today beyond the walls of your jail, tapping my cane to get your attention: Captives, hear me—you still have family in the world beyond this place. Escape can happen in countless ways.

Long ago, I used all my cleverness to make sure my own cell stayed shut. I arranged for chains to be hidden inside pies and sent in to me, and I loudly announced my schemes where the guards could hear them. Yet fresh ideas kept coming anyway; sometimes the new, oversized locks pulled the hinges out of shape, and sometimes a foolish guard simply forgot and left the keys behind.

While I was confined, I imagined the constellations: beasts made from patterns of stars, their bones formed by the dark spaces among bright points, champions who are visible only through what is absent. In that same way, freedom kept chewing at the edge of my mind. It is like being out in daylight on wide hills: you may walk past an antelope without realizing it, then glance back, and even before your eyes find it, you sense that the grass is not quite right. Then suddenly you see it.

That is how everything in this world lies in wait.

Now I will say only a little more before I leave: Tell everyone to hold on to their names, and later, when we meet again, to help others remember theirs. Tell the children to weep if they must, and afterward to sleep wherever they can curl themselves up. And if some among us lose the way, if some cannot make the whole journey, remember this: a day will arrive when everything we have spoken and everything we have wished for will come right. That shape in the grass will be there.
outputs.L3:
The speaker stands outside the prison walls and calls out to those held inside, urging them to listen. Though the walls are high and the gates are locked, the speaker insists that the prisoners are not as powerless as they may feel. They have connections beyond the prison, ties to people and memories, to one another, and to the world outside. There are many possible paths toward escape, even if those paths are not yet visible. The speaker wants them to remain alert, to recognize that freedom may come through unexpected openings, through courage, solidarity, patience, or imagination.

The speaker then remembers a time when they, too, tried to remain imprisoned. They accepted the locks, the chains, and the watchful jailers, perhaps believing that captivity was unavoidable or even safer than the uncertainty of freedom. Yet freedom would not leave them alone. It kept returning in small but persistent ways, slipping through cracks, breaking through barriers, and making itself known despite every attempt to shut it out. No lock was strong enough to silence it completely, and no jailer could prevent it from reaching the human spirit.

To describe this freedom, the speaker turns to images of mystery and invisibility. Freedom is compared to hidden constellations, patterns of stars that exist even when clouds or darkness prevent people from seeing them. It is also like unseen creatures moving beyond the edge of sight, alive even when unnoticed. In this way, freedom exists first in absence, longing, and imagination. It may be invisible for a time, but that does not mean it is unreal. Before it becomes a fact in the world, it lives in memory, desire, and the shared dreams of those who refuse to forget it.

The speaker then gives the prisoners practical and emotional instructions. They must remember their names, because their identities are a source of strength. They must care for the young, protecting them not only physically but also by teaching them who they are and where they come from. They must remind one another of their dignity, their histories, and their purpose. In a place designed to strip them of selfhood, the act of remembering becomes a form of resistance.

Finally, the speaker offers hope. They acknowledge that some may be lost before freedom arrives, and that not everyone may live to see the promised future. Still, the speaker believes that their words, hopes, and struggles will not disappear. A time will come when what they have spoken in darkness will be fulfilled in the open air. Their longing for freedom will become more than a dream; it will become a reality carried forward by those who remember, endure, and continue the work.
outputs.L4:
The speaker stands outside the prison walls and addresses those confined within, speaking to them across the distance that separates freedom from captivity. Rather than describing imprisonment only as a place of suffering, the speaker fills the scene with memory, light, and images from nature. The prisoners are reminded that beyond the walls there are skies, stars, winds, fields, and living things that continue to move and shine. These images suggest that the world has not forgotten them, and that their own inner lives cannot be completely contained by bars or stone.

Memory becomes a form of resistance in the poem. The speaker urges the prisoners to remember who they are, where they come from, and the bonds that still connect them to others. Even if their bodies are locked away, their identities remain alive through remembrance. The celestial imagery—stars, moonlight, or the vastness of the sky—creates a sense of guidance and permanence. These lights above the prison suggest that hope exists beyond immediate suffering and that a larger order of justice may still be present, even when it is difficult to see.

The natural metaphors also deepen the poem’s message of hope. Nature often works quietly and invisibly: seeds grow underground, dawn approaches before it is seen, and seasons change even after long winters. In the same way, liberation may already be approaching, though it may not yet be obvious to those who suffer. The poem suggests that freedom is not merely a distant dream but something inevitable, something hidden in plain sight. It may exist in memory, in shared faith, in solidarity, and in the refusal to let oppression define the soul.

Ultimately, the poem offers comfort without denying pain. It recognizes the loneliness and hardship of imprisonment, but it also insists that captivity is not the final truth. The speaker’s words become a bridge between those outside and those inside, promising that the prisoners are not abandoned. Through remembrance, collective identity, and belief in a future reunion, the suffering are encouraged to endure. The poem’s central hope is that freedom will come, and that when it does, those who have remained faithful to themselves and to one another will be able to meet again in dignity and light.
outputs.L5:
**Today, Prisoners, and the Hope for Change**

Today, prisoners around the world live behind walls that separate them from society, their families, and the lives they once knew. Some are serving time for serious crimes, while others may be waiting for trial or struggling within unfair systems. Prison is often seen only as punishment, but it can also be a place where people reflect, learn, and begin to change.

Prisoners are still human beings, and many need education, mental health support, and opportunities to build better futures. When prisons focus only on isolation and punishment, people may leave worse than when they entered. But when they offer rehabilitation, job training, counseling, and dignity, prisoners have a better chance to return to society and live responsibly.

Today, the way we treat prisoners says a lot about our values. Justice is important, and victims deserve respect and protection. At the same time, society benefits when prisoners are given a real chance to grow, make amends, and rebuild their lives. A fair system should balance accountability with humanity.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem in the style of William Stafford, addressing prisoners from outside a prison, using imagery of escape, constellations, antelopes in grass, and ending with a quiet message of hope.
counterfactuals.output:
Friends inside, I am standing where the road gives up and becomes dust, where the fence gathers the evening in its wires. I can’t see you, but I know the small windows are taking turns holding your faces. Above us the first stars loosen themselves from daylight, not as keys exactly, but as little openings the dark forgot to close.

Out here the grass keeps making its green arguments. Antelopes step through it as if the earth had left no record of fear. Their bodies lean forward, all listening and flight, and for a moment the whole field seems to be escaping—blade by blade, breath by breath—without ever leaving where it is.

I want to tell you the constellations have not been assigned to anyone. The Dipper, the Hunter, the long river of milk across the sky: they pass over the yard, the towers, the count, the locked doors, and do not stop. Somewhere beyond the hill a creek is practicing its way around stone. Somewhere a gate is only a shape the morning will pass through.

So tonight, if you can, look up. Let the sky come quietly to your window. Let it stand there with you, saying nothing much, only this: the world is still larger than what holds you, and it has not forgotten your name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical monologue where a former prisoner speaks to those still trapped, telling them there are many ways to escape and that freedom is waiting everywhere.
counterfactuals.output:
Listen—  
I speak to you from the other side of the wall.

Not because I was stronger,  
not because the iron softened for me,  
not because the watchmen slept longer than usual—  
but because somewhere, somehow,  
I learned the truth the bars were built to hide:

There is more than one way out.

Some doors open with a key.  
Some with patience.  
Some with a whisper passed hand to hand in the dark.  
Some with a song remembered so fiercely  
it becomes a road beneath your feet.

I have seen cracks become windows.  
I have seen silence become a ladder.  
I have seen a single thought—  
no bigger than a seed—  
split stone.

So do not believe the cell  
when it tells you it is the whole world.  
Do not believe the ceiling  
when it lowers its gray face  
and says the sky is dead.  
The sky is not dead.  
It is waiting.

Freedom is not one gate in one direction.  
It is hidden in every direction.

It is in the footstep you take  
when fear orders you to kneel.  
It is in the name you keep  
when they try to rename you.  
It is in the breath you save  
for tomorrow.  
It is in the hand beside yours,  
warm in the cold,  
proving you are not alone.

I found freedom first  
not in the open field,  
but in the refusal  
to let my soul be counted  
among their possessions.

And after that—  
the wall was only a wall.

Oh, my friends still in shadow,  
my brothers and sisters of locked rooms,  
my bright ones buried under years—  
listen for the hinges of the world.  
They are everywhere.

A loose brick.  
A moonless hour.  
A memory of water.  
A guard who doubts.  
A storm.  
A kindness.  
A map drawn on the inside of the heart.  
A moment when the body says, Now.  
A moment when the spirit says, Always.

Do not ask only, “Where is the exit?”  
Ask, “What has already begun to open?”

For freedom is a river under the prison.  
Freedom is grass growing through concrete.  
Freedom is the bird that lands on barbed wire  
and sings as if it were a branch.  
Freedom is the dawn practicing its gold  
even on the faces of locked doors.

I am not calling you to despair.  
I am calling you by your true names.

You who have endured—  
you are not the cage.  
You who have waited—  
you are not the waiting.  
You who have been numbered—  
you are not the number.  
You are the road remembering itself.  
You are the fire learning its shape.  
You are the sea,  
and every wall is temporary  
before the sea.

When you come out—  
and you can come out in a thousand ways—  
the world will not be empty.  
It will rush toward you:  
wind, bread, rain, voices,  
the wild green laughter of trees,  
the endless astonishment of space.

Freedom is waiting in the streets.  
Freedom is waiting in the fields.  
Freedom is waiting in the first deep breath  
that belongs only to you.

And if you cannot see it yet,  
borrow my sight:

I have been where you are.  
I have worn the dark like a second skin.  
I have counted days on stone.  
I have forgotten the sound of my own footsteps  
until the earth gave them back.

Now I tell you—  
the world is wider than their walls.  
The future is not locked.  
The door is not the only door.

Hold fast.  
Look close.  
Listen low.

There are many ways to escape,  
and freedom—  
freedom is waiting everywhere.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an AI-generated poem about captivity and liberation, with surreal details like chains smuggled in pies, jailers forgetting keys, star-formed animals, and a hidden antelope in the grass.
counterfactuals.output:
In the prison orchard, clocks grew pears,  
and pies arrived at dusk with iron crusts—  
chains coiled inside them like sleeping snakes,  
warm with cinnamon, cold with rust.

The jailers forgot their keys on the moon,  
left them ringing in its cratered bowl,  
then wandered the halls with empty belts  
and dreams leaking out through their buttonholes.

At midnight, the sky bent low to listen.  
Stars unstitched themselves from the dark  
and gathered into luminous beasts:  
a wolf of sparks, a swan of fire,  
a horse whose mane was a comet’s arc.

We broke our locks with a song too small  
for any guard to hear—  
a hummingbird note, a silver thread,  
a door becoming a clearing.

Beyond the walls, the grass was whispering.  
There, hidden in the green’s deep sleeve,  
an antelope lifted its lantern eyes  
as if it had waited centuries  
to teach our frightened feet to leave.

And when we ran, the chains behind us  
turned to vines, then rain, then light;  
the pies cooled empty on the tables,  
the jailers slept without their names,  
and the star-formed animals led us  
past the last fence of night.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Rewrite a hopeful prison-break speech as a literary free-verse poem, mixing humor, dreamlike imagery, and a final reassurance that everything hoped for will someday be all right.
counterfactuals.output:
Friends,  
listen—

the walls have been practicing  
their stern faces for years,  
but even stone gets tired  
of pretending it is permanent.

Tonight, hope is not a key, exactly.  
It is more like a spoon  
with delusions of grandeur,  
a moonbeam in work boots,  
a mouse with a clipboard  
inspecting the foundations of despair.

We have dreamed bigger than this place.  
We have dreamed of doors  
remembering they are only wood and hinges,  
of watchtowers blinking first,  
of the yard blooming overnight  
with ladders made of sunflowers.

Somewhere beyond the wire,  
the world is warming its hands  
over the little fire of morning.  
Somewhere, a river is rehearsing our names.  
Somewhere, breakfast is happening  
without permission,  
and coffee is being poured  
with the reckless generosity  
of a free civilization.

So laugh, if you can—  
quietly, like contraband thunder.  
Laugh at the lock  
for thinking metal can understand  
the weather inside a human heart.

We are not only what has been taken.  
We are not only these numbers,  
these bunks,  
these fluorescent moons buzzing overhead.

We are maps folded under skin.  
We are songs the bars cannot memorize.  
We are the stubborn green fuse  
beneath winter’s boot.

And when the hour comes—  
whether by tunnel, miracle, mercy,  
or the slow official incompetence  
of doom misfiling our paperwork—  
we will step out

not as ghosts,  
not as shadows,  
but as people carrying dawn  
in both hands.

Hold on.

Hold on to the impossible  
until it becomes embarrassed  
and changes its name to tomorrow.

All that we have hoped for—  
the open road,  
the unlocked sky,  
the faces waiting in the light—  
will find us.

Not all at once, perhaps.  
Not without scars.  
But someday,  
somehow,  
the world will soften.

And everything we have hoped for  
will be all right.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a meditative, Stafford-esque passage beginning “Today outside your prison I stand” and ending with an image of “that form in the grass.”
counterfactuals.output:
Today outside your prison I stand  
with my hands empty, as the trees are empty  
after wind has taken what it wanted.

The road behind me is quiet.  
It has carried all morning the small dust  
of ordinary going-on, and now it waits,  
as if a road too could listen.

I do not know what door will open,  
or whether any door is meant for me.  
I have brought no argument, no key,  
only the slow weather of being here.

A bird crosses the wire and is gone.  
The wall keeps its gray thought to itself.  
Somewhere within, a name is held  
like water in a covered cup.

I think of how the world continues  
beside our sorrow: ants in their dark errands,  
grass leaning back after a footstep,  
clouds passing without forgiveness or blame.

If you came out now, we might not speak.  
We might walk a little along the ditch  
where sunlight gathers in broken bottles  
and makes of them a brief, mistaken fire.

There is so much I never understood—  
how a heart can be locked in daylight,  
how silence can grow heavy enough  
to bend a life toward the ground.

Still, I stand here. Still, the afternoon  
lays its calm hand on the fields.  
And near the fence, where no one has looked,  
the wind keeps touching that form in the grass.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
